script.opening: (Direct, slightly agitated, wants a straight answer.) "Right, I need you to be honest with me. My HRT has genuinely given me my life back — but my friend said I'm 'basically asking for breast cancer', and there was a big headline about it. So just give it to me straight: does HRT cause breast cancer, yes or no? Should I stop?"

facts.text: "Awful. The symptoms were severe. Now I'm sleeping, I'm working, I feel like me again." Had 20 flushes a day and was nearly signed off work.
Oestrogen gel and micronised progesterone continuously (no bleeds). "I'd have to check exactly when I started" — about two years ago, at 52. Bleeding: none for over a year.

"Not that I know of, no changes, and yes, I go for screening" — no family history of breast or ovarian cancer, no breast lumps or changes, mammogram 8 months ago normal. BMI 29. Drinks about 14 units a week. Non-smoker. Had two children, breastfed both.
HRT only. No allergies. No clots, migraine with aura or liver disease.
Office manager, divorced, two adult children. Her friend's sister had breast cancer last year.
If asked how the comment made her feel: "Guilty, honestly. Like I've been reckless for feeling better."

Wants a yes/no and gets impatient with waffle. If the doctor explains with absolute numbers: "So out of a thousand, most women on it don't get breast cancer because of it." and "That's so different from the headline." Wants to keep going: "I want to keep going. But I want to keep an eye on it." Asks: "And if I change my mind?" If told a flat "no, it's safe", she pushes back: "That's not what the paper said."

ice.ideas: "Maybe my friend is right and I'm asking for breast cancer."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — guilt at feeling better, as if she has been reckless; torn between the life HRT has given back and the fear of harm; her friend's sister's cancer is on her mind.
ice.expectations: "A straight answer — and whether I should stop."

cues: "Yes or no?" — wants honesty, not reassurance.
"Given me my life back." — the benefit side of the balance.
"Like I've been reckless." — guilt to address.

checkpoints.text: Answers HONESTLY without a misleading yes/no — an increased risk with COMBINED HRT (duration-dependent; falls after stopping but some excess persists more than 10 years, MHRA 2019); smallest increase with OESTROGEN-ONLY (NG23: little/no change) — avoiding both false reassurance and scaremongering
Communicates risk in ABSOLUTE terms / NATURAL FREQUENCIES ("extra cases per 1000 women") rather than relative percentages, which exaggerate the perceived change

CONTEXTUALISES the risk with a sourced comparison (BMS Fast Facts 2025: similar in size to the risk linked with obesity) to enable realistic weighing — without dismissing it or using unsourced alcohol comparisons

Specifies that TYPE (oestrogen-only vs sequential vs continuous combined) and DURATION matter, that ROUTE matters for VTE rather than breast risk, and that any lower breast risk with micronised progesterone is uncertain (MHRA 2019 found the increase with any progestogen)
Reconnects to HER — the real benefit ("given her life back"), bone protection, and individual risk factors (family history, alcohol, BMI) — framing a VALUES-based, revisitable decision
Validates that the question is sensible, reassures she is not "asking for cancer", and addresses the fear from the friend/headline directly
Checks her understanding of the numbers and supports her autonomy to decide with clarity rather than fear

Safety-nets and follows up: offers written information/decision support, reviews the decision over time, advises on modifiable risk factors, and reminds her to report unscheduled bleeding — informed choice, not a scare or a dismissal

worked.txt: "That’s a completely fair question, and I’ll be straight with you — but a true ‘yes or no’ would actually mislead you. The honest answer is a number, and once you see it I think it’ll feel very different from the headline."

"There is a small extra risk with the combined type of HRT, and it goes up the longer you take it. To put a number on it: out of 1000 women who start at around 50 and never take HRT, about 59 get breast cancer over the next 20 years. Five years of the combined type adds about 20 more over that time — so about 79 instead of 59. Ten years adds about 33, so about 92. After stopping, the extra risk falls, but a little of it lasts more than ten years. Oestrogen alone, for women without a womb, adds about 10 for five years."

"To weigh that fairly: the British Menopause Society puts that extra risk at about the same size as the extra risk that comes with being obese — something we talk about, but don’t panic about. I’m not dismissing it; I’m helping you see it in proportion."

"We can also keep things under review — using the lowest dose that controls your symptoms, and reviewing at least once a year how long you stay on it. You may read that body-identical progesterone is safer for the breast; honestly, that isn’t proven, so I won’t promise it."

"And here’s the part that matters most: you said HRT gave you your life back. That benefit is real and counts. Only you can weigh that benefit against those numbers — there’s no single right answer for every woman — so it’s genuinely your call, you can change your mind anytime, and we’ll look at it again at every review."

"You are not ‘asking for cancer’. Let’s keep an eye on the modifiable things like alcohol, attend your screening, and tell me about any unexpected bleeding. I’ll give you something written to look at, and we can revisit this whenever you like."

f.learning: "Does HRT cause breast cancer?" is a risk-communication station where the mark lies in translating evidence into meaningful numbers and supporting an informed choice, not in a yes/no. Answer honestly: there is an increased risk of breast cancer with combined (oestrogen + progestogen) HRT that rises with duration and falls after stopping but persists in part for more than 10 years (MHRA Drug Safety Update, August 2019), while oestrogen-only HRT (for women without a uterus) carries the smallest increase (about 10 extra per 1000 over 20 years for 5 years from 50 — NICE NG23 discussion aid, 2024) — avoiding both false reassurance and the headline’s scaremongering. The core skill is to express risk in absolute terms and natural frequencies ("of 1000 women starting around 50 who never use HRT, about 59 develop breast cancer over 20 years; five years of combined HRT adds about 20 extra cases, ten years about 33" — NICE NG23 discussion aid, 2024) rather than relative percentages, which make the change sound far larger, and to contextualise it with a sourced comparison — British Menopause Society Fast Facts (2025): the excess risk with 5 years of combined HRT at 50–59 is similar in size to that linked with obesity — not to dismiss it but to let her weigh it realistically and act on modifiable factors (weight, alcohol, activity). Be specific that type (oestrogen-only vs sequential vs continuous combined; any lower breast risk with micronised progesterone is uncertain, as MHRA 2019 found increased risk with any progestogen), duration and — for VTE rather than breast — route matter, and that the regimen can be tailored to minimise risk. Reconnect to her: the real benefit (symptom relief that "gave her life back", bone protection) and her individual risk profile, framing a values-based, revisitable decision, reviewed at least once a year, in which she weighs the benefit she actually feels against the honest absolute numbers. Validate the question, reassure she is not "asking for cancer", support her autonomy with clarity, offer written decision support and review, and remind her to report unscheduled bleeding. NICE NG12 (Suspected cancer: recognition and referral, last updated April 2026) is not the subject, though the bleeding safety-net still applies.

knowledge.summary: The honest answer is a number, not a yes or no. Systemic HRT carries a small, duration-dependent increase in breast cancer risk, largest with combined HRT; in absolute terms most women who take it are not harmed by it.

points.t: NICE NG23 discussion aid (2024): of 1000 women starting around 50 who never use HRT, about 59 are diagnosed with breast cancer over the 20 years to age 69 (about 1 in 17).

NICE NG23 discussion aid (2024): over the same 20 years, 5 years of combined HRT gives about 79 per 1000 (20 extra) and 10 years about 92 (33 extra); 5 years of oestrogen-only gives about 69 (10 extra).

MHRA 2019 found increased risk with all systemic HRT, whatever the oestrogen, progestogen or route; no increase was found with low-dose vaginal oestrogen. Some excess risk persists for more than 10 years after stopping. NICE NG23 states oestrogen-only HRT is associated with little or no change in risk, and combined HRT with an increase related to duration.
Use natural frequencies (“out of 1000 women like you”) with the same time frame for baseline and extra cases. A percentage increase sounds far larger than the absolute change.

BMS Fast Facts (2025): the excess risk with 5 years of combined HRT at 50–59 is of a similar size to that linked with obesity. Modifiable factors — weight, alcohol, activity — are worth addressing whatever she decides.
Review HRT at least yearly; continue NHS breast screening; report breast changes. NICE NG23 (April 2026): report unscheduled bleeding beyond the first 6 months or 3 months after a change.

model.text: Hello Frances, I’m Dr Lee. What’s on your mind today?

I need you to be honest. My HRT has given me my life back, but a friend said I’m basically asking for breast cancer, and there was a big headline. So does HRT cause breast cancer — yes or no? Should I stop?

That’s a completely fair question, and I will be straight with you. A plain yes or no would actually mislead you — the honest answer is a number. Can I show you the numbers, and then we’ll work out together what they mean for you?
model.why: Honours the question; sets up risk communication

model.text: Go on then.
First, tell me what HRT has done for you — what was life like before?
model.why: Establishes the benefit side of the scales in her words

model.text: Awful. The symptoms were severe. Now I’m sleeping, I’m working, I feel like me again.

That matters, and we’ll keep it in the picture. I can see which HRT you’re on from your repeat list — it includes a progestogen as well as oestrogen, which is the type with a small extra breast risk. How long have you been taking it?
model.why: Type and duration determine the figures

model.text: I’d have to check exactly when I started.
Is there any breast cancer in your close family, and have you noticed any breast changes? Are you up to date with breast screening?
Not that I know of, no changes, and yes, I go for screening.
What did your friend’s comment leave you feeling?
model.why: Explores the emotional driver behind the question

model.text: Guilty, honestly. Like I’ve been reckless for feeling better.
You haven’t been reckless. You made a sensible choice for severe symptoms, and asking this question is sensible too. Let’s put real numbers on it.

Picture 1000 women aged 50. Over the next 20 years, about 59 will get breast cancer without ever taking HRT. If they each take five years of combined HRT, about 20 more will. So about 79 instead of 59.
model.why: NICE NG23 discussion aid (2024) absolute figures as natural frequencies

model.text: So out of a thousand, most women on it don’t get breast cancer because of it.

Exactly. Two more honest points. The risk grows with the number of years you take it — ten years adds about 33 per 1000 rather than 20, so we’ll check your start date and use it. And some of the extra risk lasts for years after stopping, so stopping now doesn’t reset it to zero.

For comparison, the extra risk from five years of combined HRT is about the same as the extra risk linked to obesity in your fifties. I’m not saying that to dismiss it — it’s to help you see it alongside risks people live with every day.

Oestrogen on its own — for women who’ve had a hysterectomy — carries less risk, and vaginal oestrogen for dryness hasn’t been shown to raise it. Patches versus tablets makes a difference to clot risk, not breast risk.
That’s so different from the headline.
Headlines often use percentages — “a 30% increase” sounds terrifying, but a percentage of a small number is still small. The per-1000 figure is the one that tells you what it means for you.
So, putting it together: on one side, severe symptoms now controlled and your bones protected. On the other, a small extra risk that grows with time. What feels right to you?
I want to keep going. But I want to keep an eye on it.

That’s a very reasonable decision. We’ll review each year — whether you still need it, and the lowest dose that works. Anything you can do on weight, alcohol and activity lowers your risk whatever you decide. I’ll send you the NICE discussion aid so you can see the numbers again.
model.why: Annual review, modifiable factors, written information

model.text: And if I change my mind?
Then we talk again — this decision can be revisited at any time.
What will you tell your friend next time it comes up?
That out of a thousand women, a small number extra get it, it depends how long you take it, and I’ve chosen it with my eyes open.
Perfect. Keep going to breast screening, tell me about any breast lump or change, and let me know about any unexpected bleeding. Anything else today?
No. Thank you for giving me a real answer.

social.t: Headlines and friends’ comments shape decisions more than leaflets. Acknowledge them and offer a trustworthy source she can share.
Restored sleep and ability to work are real outcomes that belong in the risk–benefit discussion.

legal.t: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board (2015): patients must be told of material risks and reasonable alternatives — the breast-cancer figures are material to HRT.

professional.t: GMC decision-making and consent guidance: share information in a way the patient can understand, and respect her decision. Record the figures discussed.
Review HRT at least yearly — need, dose and her view of benefits and risks.

community.t: NICE NG23 discussion aid on HRT and breast cancer (2024); Women’s Health Concern (British Menopause Society); NHS Breast Screening Programme.

pitfalls.intro: This is a risk-communication station. Candidates fail by giving the yes or no she asks for, by using relative risk, or by retreating into vague reassurance. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: “No, the evidence has moved on — it’s safe.”
items.why: Inaccurate: MHRA 2019 found increased risk with all systemic HRT, largest with combined.
items.fix: “There is a small extra risk with your type — here’s how small, per 1000 women.”

items.fail: Quoting only a relative risk or a percentage increase.
items.why: Relative figures inflate perceived risk and don’t tell her what it means for her.
items.fix: Baseline and extra cases per 1000 women, over the same time frame.

items.fail: Implying stopping removes the risk immediately.
items.why: MHRA 2019: some excess risk persists for more than 10 years after stopping.
items.fix: Say so plainly — it helps her weigh stopping against losing the benefit.

items.fail: Missing the guilt behind “should I stop?”.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.”
items.fix: “What did your friend’s comment leave you feeling?” — then address it.

items.fail: Burying the numbers in jargon — “HR 1.6, CI 1.5–1.7, E3N data”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: One picture: 1000 women, 59 anyway, 20 more with five years.

items.fail: Closing without checking understanding or planning review.
items.why: No teach-back and no follow-up are standard failing statements.
items.fix: “What will you tell your friend?” Then yearly review and the NICE discussion aid.

59 per 1000 baseline; 20 extra with five years combined; 33 with ten; persists after stopping; obesity comparison; relative vs absolute.
Her decision, annual review, modifiable factors, NICE discussion aid, teach-back, screening and bleeding safety-net.

wordPics.fail: Answers “no, it’s safe” or “yes, you should stop”; uses relative risk only; no numbers; ignores her guilt; no review.
wordPics.pass: Explains a small increased risk with combined HRT that rises with duration; gives some absolute figures; distinguishes oestrogen-only; supports her choice and arranges review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: NICE NG23 discussion-aid figures as natural frequencies with a stated time frame; persistence after stopping; a sourced everyday comparison; explains why headlines mislead; reconnects to her benefit; teach-back; she decides with confidence.

avoid.instead: "There is a small extra risk — let me show you how small, in numbers."
avoid.why: False reassurance is inaccurate and undermines trust if she reads the evidence.

avoid.dont: "It increases your risk by about a third."
avoid.instead: "About 59 in 1000 anyway; five years of combined HRT adds about 20."

avoid.dont: "If you’re worried, it’s probably safest to stop."
avoid.instead: "Let’s weigh what it’s done for you against a small risk — then it’s your call."
avoid.why: Defensive advice ignores her benefit and takes the decision away from her.

redFlags: New breast lump, skin change, nipple change or discharge — examine and refer as appropriate
Strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer — changes the individual risk
Unscheduled bleeding beyond the expected window on HRT

Guilt and fear from a friend’s comment and a headline
Weight, alcohol and activity as modifiable factors
ice: Concern: she has been reckless and should stop
Expectation: a straight yes or no

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Combined HRT carries a small increase in breast cancer risk that rises with duration and partly persists after stopping; in absolute terms, about 20 extra cases per 1000 women over 20 years for five years’ use from 50 (NICE NG23 discussion aid, 2024).
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Out of 1000 women your age, about 59 will get breast cancer over 20 years anyway. Five years of your type of HRT adds about 20 to that. So most women on it are not harmed by it — but the risk is real, and it grows the longer you take it.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked for honesty, and you’re not reckless — you made a sensible choice. Here are the real numbers so you can decide.”
management.psychosocial: Remove guilt, reconnect to her benefit, and give her words to use with her friend.
sharedPlan: Her choice: continue, reduce or stop — with the figures to hand
Annual review of need and lowest effective dose
Modifiable factors: weight, alcohol, activity; NICE discussion aid
safetyNet: Breast lump or change — see us promptly; continue breast screening
Unscheduled bleeding beyond the expected window — report promptly

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a risk-communication station. Candidates fail by giving the yes or no she asks for, by using relative risk, or by retreating into vague reassurance. Each pattern below is fixable.

items.fail: “No, the evidence has moved on — it’s safe.”
items.why: Inaccurate: MHRA 2019 found increased risk with all systemic HRT, largest with combined.
items.fix: “There is a small extra risk with your type — here’s how small, per 1000 women.”

items.fail: Quoting only a relative risk or a percentage increase.
items.why: Relative figures inflate perceived risk and don’t tell her what it means for her.
items.fix: Baseline and extra cases per 1000 women, over the same time frame.

items.fail: Implying stopping removes the risk immediately.
items.why: MHRA 2019: some excess risk persists for more than 10 years after stopping.
items.fix: Say so plainly — it helps her weigh stopping against losing the benefit.

items.fail: Missing the guilt behind “should I stop?”.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to the patient’s cues.”
items.fix: “What did your friend’s comment leave you feeling?” — then address it.

items.fail: Burying the numbers in jargon — “HR 1.6, CI 1.5–1.7, E3N data”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: One picture: 1000 women, 59 anyway, 20 more with five years.

items.fail: Closing without checking understanding or planning review.
items.why: No teach-back and no follow-up are standard failing statements.
items.fix: “What will you tell your friend?” Then yearly review and the NICE discussion aid.
